title: \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) conjecture
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every partial order \(\mathrm{P}=([n],\le _{\mathrm{P}})\) that is not a total order, do there exist incomparable elements \(x,y\in [n]\) such that \(e(\mathrm{P})/3\le e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y)\le 2e(\mathrm{P})/3\)?
why: Asks for the sharp universal quality of a comparison when sorting with partial information. It connects uncertainty among compatible rankings to an extremal property of every finite partial order.

progress.text: Brightwell–Felsner–Trotter establish the general balance bound \((5- \sqrt{5})/10\).
Chan–Pak survey distinguishes the open universal conjecture from established structural cases.
Aires–Kahn prove stronger balance under width and other size hypotheses.
Gupta reports exhaustive verification of Gold Partition through fourteen elements, implying the target in that finite range.

definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). A partial order \(\le _{\mathrm{P}}\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation. Distinct x,y are incomparable when neither \(x\le _{\mathrm{P}} y\) nor \(y\le _{\mathrm{P}} x; \mathrm{P}\) is a total order when no such pair exists. A linear extension is a bijection \(\mathrm{L}:[n]\to [n]\) with \(\mathrm{L}(a)<\mathrm{L}(b)\) whenever \(a\le _{\mathrm{P}} b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(\mathrm{P})\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(\mathrm{P})=|E(\mathrm{P})|\), and \(e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y)=|\{\mathrm{L}\in E(\mathrm{P}):\mathrm{L}(x)<\mathrm{L}(y)\}|\). Equivalently choose L uniformly from \(E(\mathrm{P})\), so the displayed interval requires \(\Pr [\mathrm{L}(x)<\mathrm{L}(y)]\in [1/3,2/3]\), including endpoints. The pair x,y may depend on the entire poset. This is an existence proposition over all finite orders, with no width, height or representation restriction and no algorithmic requirement. Width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements; height is the largest size of a totally ordered subset. For context, the balance constant is \(\beta (\mathrm{P})=\max _{x\ne y} \min \{e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y),e_{\mathrm{P}}(y,x)\}/e(\mathrm{P})\); this card uses \(\beta\) to avoid conflicting \(\delta\) conventions across sources.

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequalities for at least one incomparable pair in every finite non-total order, or exhibit a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair has probability outside \([1/3,2/3]\). All probabilities refer to the uniform distribution on its full set of linear extensions.

sentences: A partial order records known comparisons, and its linear extensions are all compatible complete rankings.
The conjecture asks whether every finite non-total order has an incomparable pair that appears in either relative order in at least one third of all extensions.
The extensions are weighted uniformly, and both endpoints of the interval are allowed.
A three-element order with only one comparison shows that the constant one third cannot be improved universally.
A resolution would identify the sharp balance guarantee for a comparison in sorting with partial information.
